title: A State Court Authorization for a Security Test, but the Sheriff Says the Contract Is Void
dek: A state court's authorization doesn't cover a county courthouse, turning a commissioned security test into burglary. Even after all charges are dropped, the arrest record lingers—the justice system can pay damages but cannot restore a clean name.
why: It explains the fragility of an 'authorization contract' more clearly than any exploit: the building's owner can override all paperwork, and judicial accountability is nearly blocked by immunity. Security contractors and vendor-side project teams should pause here.
who: Physical security testing teams, legal counsel for security service vendors, and anyone who enters a site with a client's authorization; also tech founders who want to understand the U.S. game of judicial immunity.
skip: The first half hour's lock-picking techniques and access-control details are more technically entertaining; if you're impatient, skip to 35:18 to see the conflict erupt.

points.h: An oral agreement is no authorization at all
points.body: The rulebook is only 28 pages, which makes it easy to think the written contract locks everything down. But Gary says the truly detailed agreements were almost all made orally over the phone; if everything were written down, the contract would be a hundred pages long and no one would sign it. That compromise planted a landmine: when they later tested the Dallas County Courthouse, the oral agreement's scope did not cover that building—so procedurally they walked into a building 'without authorization.' The sheriff's later claim of 'no authorization' stems not from the technology but from a contract that couldn't cover every spoken conversation.

points.h: The building's owner outranks the authorization letter
points.body: Before the sheriff arrived, they were confident because the contract clearly stated state court authorization. But the sheriff's reaction was only: they don't own this courthouse, I don't care if you have a contract. Gary and Justin realized that the right to use a building and the right to contract are separate; no matter how formal the state court's contract, it cannot make entry decisions for the county courthouse's owner. The atmosphere shifted from relaxed to arrest, and they hadn't even worried earlier because no tester in the industry had ever been prosecuted. This time was different.

points.h: The judge heard the truth as a lie
points.body: The judge told Gary, 'You must think I'm stupid'—her reasoning was: if the state government had authorized this test, she, as a state employee, would have known; since she didn't know, it could only be a lie. Gary later said this judge, who faces criminals' lies daily, could no longer distinguish truth from falsehood. A reasonable but dangerous logic: in a courtroom full of lies, an alibi-like contract appears even more false. Professional reports and legal procedures were all useless in this scenario.

points.h: Dropped charges do not erase the record
points.body: On January 30, 2020, all charges were dropped, but their criminal records will forever show they were arrested for burglary. Justin said they were deprived of rights without due process—in many U.S. background checks, an arrest record is as visible as a conviction. A dismissal only means no prosecution; it cannot erase the consequences of that arrest: job hunting, customs, security clearance—this episode follows them. The innocence won in a criminal fight is only half won.

points.h: The government uses immunity to refuse responsibility for its own mistakes
points.body: Accountability is harder than imagined. They wanted to sue the sheriff, the prosecutor, and the judge, but the system presented two walls: qualified immunity protects individuals acting in official capacity, and sovereign immunity says the government cannot be sued without its consent. The state court first dismissed—because the state government was the defendant; the federal court then kicked the case back to the state, which dismissed again. This is not judging a case but a system with no entry point for 'the government was wrong.' The only thing victims can sue is the position, not the person in it; the sheriff personally pays not a cent. Judicial checks and balances here become an idle adjective.

points.h: Winning the judicial lottery buys back a little dignity
points.body: Almost every wrongful arrest case dies the same way: over 95% are dismissed on qualified immunity, and most of the rest end in zero damages or government victory. The chance of getting more than fifty thousand dollars in damages is like winning the lottery, unless you were wrongly held for weeks or months. Gary and Justin were held only one night, but their evidence was airtight, and at the arbitration they finally got a rare public statement: it wasn't a question of whether they would win, but how much they would get. Nearing trial, the county offered $300,000 each, a total of $600,000 to settle. But for them, that money cannot buy back the half-life already written into the record.

terms.def: Protects government officials from being sued for actions taken in their official capacity unless they clearly violated constitutional or statutory rights.
A legal doctrine that prevents private parties from suing the government without its consent.
